source.title: 4+3 Phases of Compute-Optimal Neural Scaling Laws
source.authors: Elliot Paquette; Courtney Paquette; Lechao Xiao; Jeffrey Pennington

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and numerically examines scaling and compute-optimal allocation in a synthetic random-features model. It refines the broad scaling-law picture by identifying distinct phases with different exponents, a region without power-law decay, and finite-size and fitting-choice sensitivity. It does not test language models or held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The results concern population mean-squared risk for power-law random features trained with one-pass SGD, not LLM pretraining loss. The reported phase laws and numerical exponent measurements bear on scaling and compute-optimal allocation. Values cited from Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. are not recorded as results of this study.
record.test_reason: All results concern a synthetic power-law random-features linear regression model, trained by one-pass SGD and scored on population mean-squared risk. Every version is about language-model pretraining loss and allocation (V1 names language models; V3 and V7 refer to the Kaplan and Hoffmann LLM laws). A toy linear model is a different kind of system, so no row bears on any version. The paper discusses the claim: it says it theoretically 'verifies' Chinchilla d⋆ ≍ f^1/2 and warns about empirically fitted laws. Its findings are recorded under fits_no_version, not as verdicts.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is largely right. Add that the authors present the f^1/2 region as theoretically verifying Chinchilla scaling. They also say that in Phases III and IV the optimizer's (SGD) noise sets the tradeoff, so a different algorithm could change the compute-optimal curves. The results are for a synthetic linear random-features model, not language models.
record.recipe_differences: Instead of measuring held-out cross-entropy in language models, the paper analyzes a synthetic power-law random-features regression model with population mean-squared loss and one-pass SGD. It derives asymptotic laws and compares them with numerical SGD and deterministic-equivalent calculations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that fitted parameter-count exponents depend on the IsoFLOP window and fitting approach. It also reports that local loss and parameter-count exponents vary across compute windows and that finite-size effects can persist, especially near a phase transition.

fits_no_version.finding: In the PLRF toy model, compute-optimal risk follows phase-dependent power laws in FLOPs across 4 phases (+3 subphases). There is no power-law decay when α+β<1/2 under v>d.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In solvable power-law random-features regression trained by one-pass SGD, compute-optimal risk is a power law in compute whose exponent depends on data and target complexity.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal parameter count d⋆ grows as a power of compute with a phase-dependent exponent. It equals f^1/2 across Phases Ib, III and IVa, which the authors call a possible universal, Chinchilla-like law.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In solvable random-features models, compute-optimal model size scales as f^1/2 over a broad region of data/target complexity, but not everywhere.

fits_no_version.finding: In the toy model, exponents fitted with Hoffmann-style IsoFLOP Approaches 1 and 2 depend on the IsoFLOP window and the approach. Local exponents drift with compute (finite-size effects), and the authors warn this applies to empirically derived laws.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Empirically fitted compute-optimal exponents can be biased by window choice and finite-size effects even when the true asymptotic law is known.

fits_no_version.finding: In Phases III and IV, SGD noise sets the compute-optimal tradeoff. Optimising the learning rate in Phase IV changes the d⋆ and loss exponents (Prop. I.1); batch size has no effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal allocation exponents can depend on the optimizer and learning-rate choice, not only on the model and data.

record.peer_reviewed: Preprint; the text says it is under review and acknowledges anonymous NeurIPS reviewers.
record.problems: The evidence is for a synthetic model and population mean-squared risk, not LLM held-out cross-entropy. The authors describe the deterministic equivalent's closeness to the random-matrix loss as a conjecture supported by numerical evidence. Phase Ic results are explicitly speculative because sharp kernel bounds are unavailable. Empirical exponent fits are sensitive to IsoFLOP windows and fitting method; numerical uncertainty intervals are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: Additional phase-plane slices and plots are not entered as separate rows where the paper does not state a specific numeric result in the text; see Figures 4, 8, 12, 15, and 16. The phase-level asymptotic laws are recorded in r1–r15.

untested.parts: Language models, held-out cross-entropy, separate N/D/C sweeps
All: no forecast of larger runs from small-run fits
LLM parameter/token allocation; Kaplan vs Hoffmann split in real models
All: no other modality, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer
LLM parameter counting, schedules, data and fitting comparisons across published laws

missing.what: Phase IV optimal-learning-rate laws: d⋆ ≍ f^((2α+2β−1)/(4αβ+2α+2β−1)), with IVa/IVb merging. Batch size has no effect on compute-optimal curves.
missing.locator: Section 3 'Compute-optimal learning rate and batch'; Section I, Prop. I.1

missing.what: Theory vs measured exponents along slices α=0.7, α=0.27 and β=0.7: loss exponents agree well; d⋆ exponents agree less well, and Approaches 1 and 2 disagree.
Finite-size drift: measured exponents still changing at d reachable with 1 A100-GPU-day; slow relaxation near the IVa→IVb boundary.
Global-window values η=0.42 and ξ=0.52, matching the averages over sliding windows.

record.verdict_notes: The reader rated the study T5 and gave labels on V1, V3 and V7. I reject these because the system is a linear toy model, not an LM, so no row bears on any version. The study is valuable as theory about mechanism and fit-dependence, so its findings are recorded under fits_no_version. The deterministic-equivalent match to SGD is a conjecture backed by numerics. The Phase Ic and α<1/4 results are speculative.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test language models, held-out cross-entropy, or separate parameter-count, token-count, and compute sweeps in LLM pretraining. Its loss is synthetic-model population risk; it reports power-law behavior for specified asymptotic regimes and a region without power-law decay.
No test of fitting a law on small runs and forecasting losses of runs orders of magnitude larger.
Tests compute-optimal parameter count versus compute in the synthetic model. Does not test an LLM parameter/token allocation or separately optimize and report the token count.
No comparison of depth, width, or architecture variants at fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer setting.
Tests phase- and fitting-choice dependence, including finite-size variation, in the synthetic model. Does not compare LLM parameter-counting conventions, data mixtures, or training schedules.

relation.reason: The study derives and numerically evaluates its own scaling laws and compares fitting approaches and compute windows. These are direct results on V7, rather than discussion alone.

tranche.reason: Sections 3.1 and J.3–J.6 demonstrate setup-dependent allocation and fitting-window-dependent exponents, with finite-size curves departing from asymptotic powers. These results bear directly on V7 and qualify stable-law interpretations; V7 is not restricted to language models.

source_check.notes: The blanket versions=none assignment misses V7 and the relevance of this regression setting to V5; no verdicts were listed to check. The supplied text is arXiv v3 dated 18 April 2025, and its synthetic population-MSE results do not establish language-model loss laws.
